title: End-user programming that ordinary users can understand and maintain

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way for people without conventional programming skills to create useful software and remain its effective authors over time. Users would describe desired behavior, inspect what the software actually does, understand its important rules, correct mistakes, and adapt it when their needs change. The defining capability is sustained understanding and maintenance, extending beyond generating an initially useful application.

Natural language could provide an entry point, with generated code serving as an internal representation of reusable behavior. The supplied CHI 2025 paper discusses that possibility. Achieving the broader concept would also require interactions that help users resolve ambiguities, examine consequences, identify exceptions, and revise behavior without having to read source code. The paper motivates this goal but does not demonstrate the full maintenance capability.

significance.text: Conditional significance: if ordinary users could independently create, inspect, correct, and maintain substantial software, many more people could author tailored computational behavior and retain control over it. Computation could become a more accessible creative medium: people could build tools around their own practices and revise those tools as their circumstances change. This is a reasoned consequence of the proposed capability, not a measured outcome of the supplied study.

Possible downstream effects include more personal and local software, faster adaptation of workflows, and less dependence on specialists for routine changes. These possibilities depend on adoption, affordability, reliability, and the amount of assistance still required. The creative-medium analogy has limits: an understandable interface would not automatically give users expertise in security, data governance, or the domain their application serves. Broader economic effects and widespread independent use are not established by the supplied evidence.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability proposed here is an interaction process that turns incomplete intentions into behavior users can understand and continue to control. The supplied experiments illustrate the underlying difficulty: descriptions sometimes omitted definitions or expressed unintended behavior, yet a receiver could still produce correct answers. Apparent success can therefore reflect a fortunate interpretation rather than a faithfully communicated rule. The study supports this concern at the level of bounded tasks; it did not directly test whether working application demonstrations conceal failures during long-term use.

Engineering synthesis: such a process would need to expose consequential assumptions, show behavior on informative examples and exceptions, and help users distinguish an intended rule from a coincidentally correct result. Users would need explanations and representations they can act on, along with ways to discover omissions they did not know to mention. Fluent dialogue or correct output alone would not demonstrate that a user understands the application's behavior.

Engineering synthesis: maintenance adds barriers beyond initial specification. Users must be able to change one rule while recognizing effects elsewhere, preserve important behavior across revisions, manage data and permissions, recover from mistakes, and respond to changing requirements. They also need workable ways to transfer responsibility or retire an application. Integrating these capabilities into an interface that remains understandable without extensive expert support is the broader breakthrough sought; the supplied study does not establish how to accomplish it.

current_state.text: Natural-language code generation and graphical end-user programming already enable some software creation. The supplied dated evidence is Madison Pickering, Helena Williams, Alison Gan, Weijia He, Hyojae Park, Francisco Piedrahita Velez, Michael L. Littman, and Blase Ur, “How Humans Communicate Programming Tasks in Natural Language and Implications for End-User Programming with LLMs,” CHI 2025, DOI: 10.1145/3706598.3713271. It examines communication about bounded information-processing tasks, including multi-step tasks in Study 2. It does not evaluate people maintaining real applications over months.

Examples helped under particular experimental conditions. Section 4.5 reports benefits for people composing task descriptions when shown examples, without a significant general benefit for receivers. Section 6 reports that the examples condition significantly improved performance when GPT-4 generated code, a benefit that did not hold in the same way for direct answering. These findings support using examples as one aid to communication, while showing that their value depends on the task and interaction. They do not establish examples as a general solution to specification or understanding.

Communication failures persisted. Section 6.6 reports missing definitions in 25 of 100 descriptions in Study 2 and 26 of 100 in Study 1, with GPT-4 sometimes apparently guessing the intended interpretation correctly. These are counts of descriptions with missing definitions, not application failure rates. They help explain why correct answers on selected cases cannot by themselves establish a complete specification or dependable user understanding.

The authors explicitly question how representative the experimental tasks are of present or possible future end-user workloads. Their discussion of generating and retaining code for future computations offers a possible architecture for reusable user-specified behavior, rather than a demonstrated system for independent longitudinal maintenance. The supplied evidence therefore establishes useful communication findings and a plausible research direction, while leaving the proposed breadth of understanding and ongoing control untested.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review had a partial extraction ending during page 20 of a stated 34 pages. The relevant main-text sections were available, and its conclusions did not depend on inspecting figures. No freshness-search record was supplied, so these materials cannot establish whether the broader capability remained unproven across the field as of November 1, 2026. That gap does not negate the dated findings or establish that no other system has made further progress.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: recruit people without conventional programming experience and have them independently create and maintain diverse, multi-step applications over several months. Applications should involve meaningful data handling, permissions, and changing requirements. The evaluation should define participant eligibility, application diversity, acceptable assistance, and success thresholds in advance. These are proposed criteria for this innovation, not established field standards.
completion_criteria.label: Nonprogrammers independently create and maintain diverse applications over several months

completion_criteria.text: Proposed tests of understanding: on previously unseen tasks and situations, participants should explain key behavioral rules, predict relevant consequences, detect seeded behavioral errors, and correct them. Evaluators should check whether explanations and predictions match actual behavior, including exceptions, and whether a correction preserves other intended behavior. Combining these measures would provide stronger evidence of understanding than either initial output correctness or users' confidence alone.
completion_criteria.label: Users demonstrate behavioral understanding and successful corrections on unseen tasks

completion_criteria.text: Proposed tests of continued control: introduce realistic requirement changes and assess whether participants can revise applications, manage permissions, recover from errors, and transfer or retire their software. Compare outcomes with current no-code and AI-assisted tools, accounting for all training, troubleshooting, expert intervention, and other support. A convincing result would show that independence persists after initial setup and through consequential changes.
completion_criteria.label: User independence persists through consequential changes against current tool baselines

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and boundaries: report task sets, participant characteristics, evaluation procedures, support accounting, and failures in enough detail for independent replication. Repeat the evaluation across different application types and user groups, and state which complexity levels and consequences remain outside the demonstrated scope. Success on finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth under those conditions, not universal comprehension or reliable maintenance of arbitrary software.
completion_criteria.label: Replicated evaluations document demonstrated breadth, limits, and full support accounting

related_concepts.text: Conceptual mapping: HCI-06, “Delegation interfaces that keep people in meaningful control of computer work,” is the closest overlap. Both require people to understand consequential behavior and intervene effectively. HCI-05 centers on authoring and maintaining reusable software; HCI-06 centers on directing and supervising delegated work. An application-building assistant could require both capabilities without making the concepts interchangeable.

Conceptual mapping: HCI-01, “A predictive science of human–computer interaction,” could inform how specification, explanation, and correction interfaces are designed and evaluated. HCI-04, “An interface that makes inaccessible software operable through a user’s chosen modality,” concerns access to software operation. HCI-05 concerns authorship and maintenance of behavior; access through a chosen modality could broaden participation but would not by itself establish that capability.

Conceptual mapping: HCI-09, “Privacy controls that remain understandable and enforceable across services,” overlaps with the permissions and data-control demands of user-created applications. HCI-10, “Lifelong personal memory augmentation with controllable evidence,” could help preserve requirements, decisions, and reasons for changes. HCI-11, “Remote collaboration with usable shared social and spatial cues,” could support shared authorship and handover. Each addresses a distinct capability that may assist software maintenance without demonstrating it.

Conceptual mapping: HCI-02, “Reliable communication and computer control after profound paralysis,” and HCI-08, “Real-time conversational interfaces across signed and spoken languages,” address communication and access capabilities that could enable more people to participate in end-user programming. HCI-03, “A general-purpose, high-fidelity interface for touch and physical force,” and HCI-07, “Everyday visual computing with perceptually convincing spatial displays,” concern interaction modalities that might support particular authoring environments. None requires the sustained comprehension and maintenance capability defining HCI-05.

Disciplinary synthesis: program synthesis and AI code generation overlap with producing executable behavior; visual programming overlaps with making that behavior inspectable and editable; software engineering overlaps with testing, revision, and maintenance. HCI-05's distinctive focus is whether people without conventional programming skills can understand and independently maintain the resulting software over time.

change_log.change: Retained HCI-05's identity and expanded the concept around sustained authorship, understanding, correction, and maintenance.
change_log.reason: The research and review identify continuing user control as the central advance beyond initial software generation.

change_log.change: Separated observed communication failures from the broader proposed maintenance challenge.
change_log.reason: The study documents incomplete descriptions and correct answers despite omissions; it did not directly test concealed failures in working applications or establish that a maintenance process is universally absent.

change_log.change: Added the condition-dependent findings about examples and the missing-definition counts.
change_log.reason: These details preserve the review's scientific distinctions and explain why selected correct outputs provide incomplete evidence of understanding.

change_log.change: Acknowledged Study 2's multi-step tasks while retaining the distinction from longitudinal application maintenance.
change_log.reason: Describing all experimental tasks as simply elementary would obscure their scope; multi-step tasks still do not establish months of maintenance.

change_log.change: Qualified the field-wide present-day claim and preserved the partial-extraction limitation.
change_log.reason: The supplied freshness record is empty, and the reviewed extraction ended during page 20 of 34. The available evidence supports dated results without settling the entire field's later status.

change_log.change: Distinguished direct conditional consequences from downstream adoption and economic possibilities.
change_log.reason: Broader authorship follows from achieving the proposed capability; widespread use and wider effects require additional evidence.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed evaluation to cover protocol definitions, actual behavioral understanding, support costs, replication, and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: These additions make the demonstration assessable without presenting proposed criteria as consensus standards or finite testing as proof of universality.

change_log.change: Mapped the concept to the supplied roster and adjacent technical fields while preserving distinctions.
change_log.reason: Related access, delegation, privacy, memory, and collaboration capabilities can contribute to end-user programming without replacing its independent maintenance objective.

unresolved_issues: The supplied materials do not settle whether any system had demonstrated the full proposed capability across the field as of November 1, 2026; no freshness-search record was provided.
The reviewed extraction is partial. Its available main-text findings support this record, but the unseen remainder cannot be characterized from the supplied review.
The representativeness of the experimental tasks for real end-user workloads remains uncertain, as the paper itself acknowledges.
No supplied evaluation establishes independent understanding and maintenance over months, including permissions, requirement changes, transfer, retirement, and total support required.
Participant eligibility, application diversity, acceptable support, success thresholds, and replication procedures remain to be specified for the proposed demonstration.

brief.title: Software people can build, understand and keep changing
possible: People without programming skills could build tools around their own needs, understand their rules, fix mistakes and adapt them as life or work changes. They could keep control of what their software does without having to read its code.
why: More people could create software tailored to their own practices and change it without depending on specialists for routine updates. Software could become a more accessible creative medium, with its users remaining its authors over time.

sources.showed: Examples sometimes helped people communicate tasks to humans and AI systems. Requests for clarification were less consistently helpful.
sources.quote:
In general, requests
for clarification did not necessarily correlate with positive outcomes.
sources.cited_for: Examples can help people express intended behavior, but conversation alone does not ensure understanding.
sources.not_established: The studies did not test whether people could understand and maintain real applications over months.

sources.who: Vijay B. Krishna and collaborators at Oregon State University
sources.showed: Spreadsheet users made more accurate changes and checked their results more thoroughly with feedback showing what needed testing after a change.
sources.quote:
This paper presents the
results of an empirical study that shows that, during
maintenance, end users using our methodology were more
accurate in making changes and did a significantly better
job of validating their spreadsheets than end users without
the methodology.
sources.cited_for: Understandable feedback can help users maintain spreadsheets.
sources.not_established: A spreadsheet modification experiment does not establish lasting independence across diverse applications.

sources.who: Michael Xieyang Liu, Advait Sarkar and collaborators
sources.showed: In a study with 24 participants, translating generated code back into editable language helped users understand the system and recover from failures during spreadsheet analysis.
sources.quote:
We find that the grounded approach improves end-users’ under-
standing of the scope and capabilities of the code-generating model,
and the kind of language needed to use it effectively.
sources.cited_for: Reflecting software behavior back in words can help users understand and correct it.
sources.not_established: The small study did not test maintenance over months or control of broader applications.

sources.showed: Beginning programmers struggled to describe tasks and revise their requests to AI systems, even when the tasks matched their skills and correctness was checked automatically.
sources.quote:
We find that students struggle significantly with this task, even
though we pose problems tailored to their skill level and test code
correctness for them.
sources.cited_for: Describing intended behavior and correcting misunderstandings remain barriers even for people with some programming training.
sources.not_established: The study did not test people without programming experience maintaining their own applications.

sources.who: Brian Bishop and Kevin McDaid, Dundalk Institute of Technology
sources.showed: In an ongoing spreadsheet study, professionals outperformed students at correcting some error types. More extensive inspection was associated with more corrections.
sources.quote:
Professionals significantly 
outperformed students in correcting certain error types.
sources.cited_for: Spreadsheet correction is measurable, and users differ in their ability to do it.
sources.not_established: Correcting deliberately inserted spreadsheet errors does not establish understanding or maintenance of diverse software.

shown: Researchers have demonstrated useful pieces of the capability. Krishna and colleagues improved spreadsheet maintenance with testing feedback. Liu, Sarkar and colleagues helped users understand and correct AI-generated behavior by translating code back into words.
missing: People without programming skills have yet to demonstrate independent creation and maintenance of diverse applications over months.
Users need to expose hidden assumptions and distinguish an intended rule from a result that happens to be correct.
Continued control must include changes, access permissions, recovery from mistakes, and handing over or retiring software.

milestones.label: Nonprogrammers independently build and maintain varied applications over months
milestones.explanation: People without programming experience would have to maintain varied applications over several months, including data, access permissions and changing needs. This would establish sustained authorship beyond initial creation.

milestones.label: Users understand behavior and correct errors in unfamiliar situations
milestones.explanation: Users would have to explain rules, predict consequences and fix deliberately inserted errors in unfamiliar situations while preserving other intended behavior. This would test understanding beyond correct outputs or confidence.

milestones.label: Independence survives consequential changes against current tools
milestones.explanation: Users would have to handle consequential changes, recovery and handover or retirement against current tools, with all help counted. This would test whether independence lasts beyond setup.

milestones.label: Independent studies reproduce results and establish their limits
milestones.explanation: Independent evaluations would have to repeat results across application types and user groups, reporting procedures, assistance and failures. This would establish the demonstrated range and its limits.

uncertain: It remains unclear how well bounded experimental tasks represent the software people would actually want to create.
Who qualifies as a nonprogrammer, how much assistance is acceptable, and what counts as success still need clear definitions.
The complexity and consequences users could reliably manage remain open questions.

page.title: End-user software engineering
page.definition: End-user software engineering concerns the quality of software people build for their own tasks, from a spreadsheet formula to an application. The goal here is for people with no prior experience writing code in a conventional programming language to create that software, explain and predict its behavior, repair faults and adapt it during continued use. They can do so without reading source code or receiving programming help from another person.

goal.need: In September 2001, 62.3% of U.S. workers who used a computer on the job worked with spreadsheets or databases. Spreadsheets inform budget, investment and tax decisions. In an audit of 25 working spreadsheets at five organizations, 70 confirmed errors affected calculated results. Staff who know the work could check those calculations and adapt local tools when procedures change, even after the original developer leaves. Faster code generation still leaves users to judge whether a rule that fits their examples also handles a new case correctly.

figures.caption: Spreadsheet maintenance after a 15-minute modification task
figures.note: Error percentages are rounded as reported. Participants were business students with mixed programming experience.

statements.body: US National Science Foundation, Foundations of Computing Processes and Artifacts programme
statements.quote: Proposals are also encouraged in the area of end-user software engineering.
statements.context: The solicitation includes understandable and adaptable programs, requirements, and software validation among the research needs.

completion.title: Nonprogrammers create, understand and maintain their software during actual use.
completion.criterion: For a declared user population and application domain, people with no prior conventional coding experience create software for their own tasks and continue using it through changed requirements and fault repair. Without reading source code or receiving programming help from another person, they correctly explain its rules and predict behavior on independently chosen, previously unseen inputs before and after changes. Independent acceptance tests confirm intended behavior; regression tests confirm that revisions preserve unaffected behavior.
completion.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion; no externally established integrated completion test was identified.
completion.basis: Searches of NSF CPA and EUSES goals, the EUSE review, ISO/IEC 25023, and end-user-programming benchmarks and preregistration records found no integrated completion test or common duration, pass rate or assistance allowance. This provisional test combines creation, understanding, fault correction and adaptation within a declared population and domain. ISO/IEC 25023 leaves compliance levels dependent on the product and users' needs.

milestones.title: A user's description produces code passing every provided task test.
milestones.criterion: The user describes a programming task from the supplied input-output examples. Code generated from that description must produce the expected output for every provided test case.
milestones.set_by: Nguyen et al., CHI 2024, section 3.2: published experimental protocol for students who had completed introductory programming; a task-level criterion rather than a population-wide target.
milestones.threshold_quote: if the generated code passed the provided tests, it was deemed correct

milestones.title: Users correctly predict a program's behavior and repair a behavioral error.
milestones.criterion: On inputs not used to construct a program, users correctly predict outputs and explain the controlling rules; they repair a behavioral fault and verify the intended result. No shared comprehension pass threshold was found. Liu et al. (2023; n=24, only 3 reporting little or no programming experience) observed debugging through editable language, without a withheld-input prediction test. Bishop and McDaid's 2008 arXiv posting reports that 13 professionals and 34 students corrected 72% and 58% of seeded spreadsheet errors, respectively.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion informed by published comprehension and debugging studies; searches found no common test combining output prediction, explanation and successful repair.

milestones.title: Users implement specified application changes without help from its original developer.
milestones.criterion: A user who took no part in developing the application implements an assigned change without assistance from its original developer. In the inventory application protocol, team members use Claude Code for changes to data entry, window behavior, error reporting or a calculation. Each task is judged by whether the requested change works.
milestones.set_by: Wang et al., Journal of Applied Clinical Medical Physics, section 3.3 and Table 3: published evaluation protocol for one radioactive-seed inventory application; a task-level criterion rather than a field-wide standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: independently modify the application using Claude Code, without any assistance from the original developer.

milestones.title: Nonprogrammers maintain a deployed application through changes arising during actual use.
milestones.criterion: A nonprogrammer changes a deployed application in response to a requirement that arises during actual use. Acceptance tests confirm that the change meets the new requirement, and regression tests confirm that behavior meant to stay the same still works.
milestones.set_by: Atlas provisional criterion extending the NSF and EUSES maintenance goal to software in use; searches found no published longitudinal acceptance threshold.

milestones.title: A user tests every executable link between a spreadsheet value and a formula that uses it.
milestones.criterion: For each executable link from an expression that defines a cell's value to a formula expression that uses it, at least one test must exercise that link. The link must contribute, directly or indirectly, to a displayed value that the user checks and marks correct. This measures coverage of the spreadsheet's calculations.
milestones.set_by: What You See Is What You Test methodology, definition-use adequacy criterion for spreadsheets
milestones.threshold_quote: each executable du-association in the spreadsheet be exercised by test data

milestones.title: A user correctly predicts the outcome of a scenario governed by trigger-action rules.
milestones.criterion: Given prewritten if-then rules and a description of events, the user selects the outcome the rules produce and explains the choice in their own words. Each scenario scores 1 for the correct prediction and 0 otherwise. Explanations are assessed separately for recognition of the bug and assumptions about the rules.
milestones.set_by: Brackenbury et al., CHI 2019, trigger-action scenario protocol and analysis
milestones.threshold_quote: whether each participant answered each scenario correctly (1) or incorrectly (0).

milestones.title: A user corrects a seeded error in a working copy of a spreadsheet.
milestones.criterion: Given a workbook with deliberately inserted errors and written rules for its data, the user locates an error and edits the workbook to correct it. Each seeded error counts as corrected only if the workbook contains the repair. The protocol reports the proportion corrected across the seeded errors.
milestones.set_by: Bishop and McDaid, spreadsheet error-correction protocol, sections 3.2 and 4.1
milestones.threshold_quote: Subjects were asked to correct any errors found directly on the spreadsheet itself.

not_found: Searches did not identify a registered protocol testing nonprogrammers' behavioral understanding throughout continued software maintenance.
The PDF download for Ekananda's preprint could not be opened, and its DOI could not be verified; its HTML text was accessible.

results.finding: All 24 participants completed three spreadsheet tasks.
results.detail: Completion was based on participants' judgment; the study did not report that generated code passed every provided input-output test. Some misinterpretations were counted as successes.
results.quote: All participants completed every task successfully.

results.finding: In a 24-participant study, grounded utterances improved users' ability to recover from system failures.
results.detail: Participants refined queries after failures, but the study did not test predictions on withheld inputs or establish the full combination of rule explanation, fault repair and verification.
results.quote:
the grounded approach improves users’ abilities to recover
from system failures

results.finding: Thirteen spreadsheet professionals corrected 72% of seeded errors.
results.detail: The study also included 34 students. It did not report a withheld-input prediction test or an assessment of explanations of controlling rules. Two professionals were software developers.
results.quote: Industry-based professional subjects corrected 72% of all seeded errors

results.finding: Of 40 treatment participants, the average keyword-understanding score was 14.1 out of 16.
results.detail: Participants adjusted a classifier and improved its accuracy, but the researchers did not grade their predicted outputs. Most participants failed every class-ratio question. The study excluded people with more than introductory programming experience, but does not state how many had none.
results.quote:
In
fact, treatment participants averaged a score of 14.1 out of 16
(88%) during the keyword assessment, suggesting they ﬁrmly
understood how the classiﬁer involved keywords—regardless
of whether the words had any semantic association with their
topics—in its reasoning.

results.finding: In a study of 153 participants, buggy infinite-loop rules were correctly predicted 46.1% of the time.
results.detail: Participants interpreted pre-written rules and explained their predictions. They did not construct or repair the rules, and the study did not test verification of a repair. Programming experience varied.
results.quote:
Participants correctly predicted outcomes significantly
more often with fixed rules — 59.9% of the time — than with
buggy rules — 46.1% of the time (OR=0.361, p=0.032).

results.finding: Three independent testers completed bug fixes and feature modifications in under 10 minutes each.
results.detail: The testers had minimal coding experience. The study does not report withheld-input predictions, explanations of controlling rules, or verification details for the repair.
results.quote: In the maintainability evaluation, three independent testers completed bug fixes and feature modifications in one to two prompts each, all in under 10 min, without guidance from the original developer.

results.finding: Among 753 participants, those reporting low programming experience scored 0.08 higher with text than Python on average debugging-question accuracy; subgroup size was not reported.
results.detail: The score averaged multiple-choice questions on output, bug location and selecting a fix. The study did not establish that users explained controlling rules, performed a repair, or verified the result. Experience was self-reported.
results.quote:

results.quote: All participants completed every task successfully.

results.finding: Among 120 beginning programmers, the mean eventual rate of generating code that passed every provided task test was 57%.
results.detail: Participants had prior coding experience through introductory computer science and could revise prompts after automated feedback. The supplied arXiv manuscript identifies 10.1145/3613904.3642706 as the DOI of the peer-reviewed CHI proceedings version.
results.quote:
The average
participant solves 57% of the assigned problems, but only after
several repeated attempts and with automatic feedback on code
correctness.

results.finding: In a workbook with 42 seeded errors, 34 accounting and finance students corrected 58% of the errors.
results.detail: The study scored correct repairs in the workbook. For one cross-sheet formula, 46% of professionals detected the error but edited the formula incorrectly.
results.quote:
Industry-based professional subjects corrected 72% of all seeded errors and student 
subjects corrected 58% of all seeded errors.

results.finding: The 67 nonprogrammers generated code passing every supplied test on an average of 1.4 of 4 Python tasks.
results.detail: The success measure allowed retries. The supplied copy is the author version of the published CHIWORK ’24 conference proceedings paper.
results.quote:
Overall, participants found
the task difficult and were only moderately successful, solving, on
average, 1.4 of 4 total problems.

results.finding: Among 77 EluciDebug participants, those given classifier explanations scored 52% higher on reasoning than controls.
results.detail: A researcher blinded to condition awarded up to two points per explanation. The source is the accepted manuscript of an ACM conference paper.
results.quote:
treatment participants scored 52% higher on the mental model
assessment than control participants ( W = 259, p < .001).

results.finding: Among 153 participants predicting outcomes from prewritten trigger-action rules, 8 of the 10 bug types tested impaired prediction accuracy.
results.detail: The sample included participants with prior programming experience. The source is a peer-reviewed CHI 2019 conference proceedings paper.
results.quote:
Eight of these bugs impaired
participants’ ability to correctly predict scenario outcomes.

results.finding: Three team members with minimal coding experience successfully implemented all 4 assigned inventory application changes.
results.quote: All tasks were completed successfully in under 10 min each, without any intervention or guidance from the original developer, and without the testers needing to read or understand the underlying source code.

results.finding: Three team members with minimal coding experience completed 4 assigned changes in an inventory application maintainability exercise.
results.detail: The maintainability exercise evaluated assigned changes. The reported clinical-use testing provides no acceptance or regression results specific to those revisions.
results.quote: In the maintainability evaluation, three independent testers completed bug fixes and feature modifications in one to two prompts each, all in under 10 min, without guidance from the original developer.

results.finding: Among 120 introductory programming students, the mean share of assigned tasks whose final generated code passed every supplied test was 57%.
results.detail: Students could revise their descriptions after automated test feedback. They had prior conventional coding experience, and the interface displayed the generated code.
results.quote: The average participant solves 57% of the assigned problems, but only after several repeated attempts and with automatic feedback on code correctness.

results.finding: Of 26 nonprogrammers using GPT-4o, 15 submitted code that passed every acceptance test for their assigned challenge.
results.detail: The source is a doctoral thesis. It identifies the underlying Study 1 article as published but does not establish its peer-review status in the supplied text.

results.finding: GPT-4-Turbo achieved 39.0% mean pass@1 across 150 tasks described by nonprogrammers.
results.detail: Test authors wrote the unit tests after collecting the descriptions. The model received API specifications and few-shot examples during generation.

results.finding: Of 920 introductory C students who attempted the first batch, 887 generated code that passed every provided test on all three tasks.
results.detail: The tool displayed generated code and test feedback during refinement. Students could revise their prompts but could not edit the generated code directly.

results.finding: In a 753-participant study, the clear-understanding, no-hint subgroup scored 12.9 percentage points higher on combined prediction and debugging questions with text than with Python.
results.detail: The reported difference combines Q2–Q4. The source gives neither a separate prediction accuracy for this comparison nor the subgroup size.
results.quote: Text-based program representations improve accuracy for users with clear understanding of the algorithmic task.

results.finding: In the unaided smart-home task, 8 of 20 participants recognized the rule conflict and correctly explained the needed changes.
results.detail: The conflict occurred where the two respiration-rate triggers overlapped and prescribed opposite actions for the same light.
results.quote:
Only 8 users out of 20 realised that there were conflicts in the rules and correctly explained 
the modifications to do to specify the expected behaviour.

results.finding: In the tool-assisted smart-home task, 8 of 20 participants correctly edited the rules to implement the requested blind-closing behavior.
results.detail: Participants used a trigger-action rule editor and simulator in a lab. Task correctness was assessed from the saved rules.
results.quote: Using the tool, 8 users successfully edited the rules to express the desired behaviour.

results.finding: Three independent testers successfully completed all four assigned changes to the seed inventory application.
results.detail: The testers completed the changes without needing to read or understand the source code.
results.quote: All tasks were completed successfully in under 10 min each, without any intervention or guidance from the original developer, and without the testers needing to read or understand the underlying source code.

results.finding: Three testers with minimal coding experience completed four assigned changes to an operational seed inventory application.
results.detail: The paper reports manual functional testing during development and clinical use. It gives no acceptance or regression test results for the assigned maintenance changes.
results.quote: In the maintainability evaluation, three independent testers completed bug fixes and feature modifications in one to two prompts each, all in under 10 min, without guidance from the original developer.

results.finding: Among 69 advanced computer science students, 21.7% exercised every executable definition-use link contributing to a validated output on the Clock spreadsheet.
results.detail: The completion rates pool both study groups. Participants tested supplied, fault-free spreadsheets with fixed formulas. The sample was drawn from advanced computer science courses, so completion by users with no prior conventional programming experience remains untested here. The source is an ICSE 2000 conference paper.

results.finding: All five StratCel users located and fixed all six formula inconsistency errors in an Excel gradebook.
results.detail: The task describes bugs originating in earlier spreadsheet use. The results also describe four other bugs as researcher-inserted and identify two previously overlooked bugs. The reported fix counts do not isolate the researcher-inserted subset.

all five participants

definition = "End-user software engineering concerns the quality of software people build for their own tasks, from a spreadsheet formula to an application. The goal here is for people with no prior experience writing code in a conventional programming language to create that software, explain and predict its behavior, repair faults and adapt it during continued use. They can do so without reading source code or receiving programming help from another person.". Reason: The definition currently makes lack of coding experience sound like a defining feature of the whole field.

goal.need = "In September 2001, 62.3% of U.S. workers who used a computer on the job worked with spreadsheets or databases. Spreadsheets inform budget, investment and tax decisions. In an audit of 25 working spreadsheets at five organizations, 70 confirmed errors affected calculated results. Staff who know the work could check those calculations and adapt local tools when procedures change, even after the original developer leaves. Faster code generation still leaves users to judge whether a rule that fits their examples also handles a new case correctly.". Reason: The student experiment reports performance on an assigned task but gives readers no measure of workplace use or of errors in software that people actually depend on.

add milestone after None: "A user tests every executable link between a spreadsheet value and a formula that uses it.". Reason: The existing milestones omit a published laboratory test of whether users systematically check the calculations on which a spreadsheet output depends.

edit m1: criterion = "The user describes a programming task from the supplied input-output examples. Code generated from that description must produce the expected output for every provided test case.". Reason: The current criterion mixes the task's pass condition with participant success rates and observations about the completeness of descriptions.

split m2 into "A user correctly predicts the outcome of a scenario governed by trigger-action rules." | "A user corrects a seeded error in a working copy of a spreadsheet.". Reason: Predicting what a faulty rule will do and changing a program to correct a fault are independently scored results.

edit m3: criterion = "A user who took no part in developing the application implements an assigned change without assistance from its original developer. In the inventory application protocol, team members use Claude Code for changes to data entry, window behavior, error reporting or a calculation. Each task is judged by whether the requested change works.". Reason: The protocol judges completion of an assigned modification, while the current criterion also reports tester counts and elapsed times.

edit m4: criterion = "A nonprogrammer changes a deployed application in response to a requirement that arises during actual use. Acceptance tests confirm that the change meets the new requirement, and regression tests confirm that behavior meant to stay the same still works.". Reason: The observation period and rollback in one repository are evidence about maintenance and do not define a passing result.
structure = parallel. Reason: Users can test, predict, repair or modify an existing program without first having generated it from a description.
